newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Economists hail new reformist Russian cabinet.
newsitem.headline: Economists hail new reformist Russian cabinet.

text.p: A group of dynamic young politicans took control of the commanding heights of the Russian economy on Monday, promising new vigour to economic reform, economists and bankers said.
The cabinet line-up is not yet complete, and some conservatives will retain their posts. But already it is clear that reformers will dominate the economic departments of the government.

"In the economic sector of the government the reformists have definitely won," said Sergei Markov, analyst at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace think tank. "Everything to do with the economy will be concentrated in the hands of reformers."
The prize for success is great. Official figures on Monday showed the Russian economy expanded for the second month running in February, suggesting the long-awaited recovery has started.
The World Bank, in a report issued on Monday, forecast the economy would grow in 1998 after zero growth this year, and could soon reach Asian "tiger" levels of six percent a year.
"However, significant reforms are still needed before Russia's new direction can be assured," it said.

Anatoly Chubais, 41, who masterminded Russia's privatisation programme and has already been named first deputy prime minister in charge of the economy, is to take on the key post of finance minister in a government whose finances are in disarray.
Boris Nemtsov, governor of Nizhny Novgorod region, which has been a showcase for pioneering reforms, becomes first deputy prime minister alongside Chubais.
Nemtsov, 37, will be responsible for tackling natural monopolies such as gas and electric power, and reforming parts of the social sector such as pensions.
Alfred Kokh, 35, a Chubais ally, who as chairman of the State Property Committee is effectively Russia's privatisation minister, is promoted to the rank of deputy prime minister.
Yakov Urinson, 52, previously deputy economy minister, takes over the Economy Ministry and also becomes deputy prime minster.
Russian markets took the appointments in their stride.
The equities market has advanced steadily since President Boris Yeltsin made it clear on March 6 that Chubais would play a key role in the new cabinet.

"The market perception has been very positive and will continue to be positive," said Catherine MacDougall, Russia analyst at London investment bank Dresdner Kleinwort Benson. "A cabinet reshuffle is a major positive step but I would like to see what will follow."

For the last 12 months Russian reforms have been virtually stalled, with the country distracted by the presidential election campaign and then leaderless as Yeltsin underwent heart surgery and contracted pneumonia.
But Chubais has a reputation as a man who gets things done, and by putting allies into other key cabinet positions can break the power of lobbyists who have acted as a drag on reforms.

The single most important task is tax reform. A collapse in government revenues has damaged relations with the International Monetary Fund, which has repeatedly cut off payments of its $10 billion loan to Russia because of worries about the budget.
The tax shortfall threatens to inflate the budget deficit, delaying the fall in interest rates which is vital if private investment is to ignite, allowing the economy to grow.
Most pressingly it means the government is simply unable to pay pensions and public-sector wages, fuelling public discontent which the communist opposition is keen to exploit.
But the list of what needs to be done does not stop there.

"There is natural monopolies, bankruptcy law, land privatisation, securities market legislation left to be dealt with," said Bill Browder, Managing Director of Hermitage Capital Management. "There is a lot that a reform government can do that requires strong hands to push it through."
